title: Two standards
hookLine: two banners: riches, honor, pride; and poverty, humiliation, humility

lines: A BANNER SHOWS WHERE YOUR SIDE IS.
HOW SMALL THE FIRST STEP IS.
cards: On a crowded field, a banner tells you where your side is standing. Lose sight of it and you can end up in the wrong company without ever deciding to.

Ignatius takes that picture, from the world he knew as a soldier, and plants two banners in front of the person praying. Two flags, two leaders, two plans. The surprise is not that one is good and one is bad.
Everyone expects that. The surprise is how small the first step is under each one.

teach.b: A standard is a banner, the flag a company gathers under. Ignatius sets up two of them on two fields.
On one, near Babylon, the enemy of our human nature sits on a throne of fire and smoke, frightening to look at, and sends his helpers into every town with a plan in three steps. First, riches.
Then the honor that comes with them: being seen, being admired.
Then, from honor, pride. And from pride, Ignatius says, the other vices follow.
On the other field, near Jerusalem, Christ stands in a lowly place, beautiful and gracious, and sends his friends out with three steps of his own.

First, poverty: poverty of spirit, and actual poverty if God chooses it for someone. Then a willingness to bear insult and being overlooked. From those comes humility, and from humility, the other virtues.
Nobody leaps into pride. It starts with wanting a little more, then wanting to be noticed for having it.
And Christ's first step is just as small: holding things lightly, the indifference from three days ago.

teach.h: NO MAN CAN SERVE TWO MASTERS.
teach.b: Jesus says it plainly in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "No man can serve two masters."

The meditation ends with three conversations, asking Our Lady, then the Son, then the Father for the grace to be received under Christ's standard, each closed with a prayer the Church already knows: a Hail Mary, the Soul of Christ, an Our Father.

how: In the second week of an Ignatian retreat, people pray the meditation on the two standards and end it with a triple colloquy to Mary, to Christ and to the Father, closing with the Hail Mary, the Anima Christi and the Our Father.

games.q: in Ignatius's meditation, you're the enemy planning how to pull someone away from God. where do you start?
o: with riches: a little more than they need.
games.why: Ignatius has the enemy start with riches, then honor, then pride. the first step looks harmless, and that's the point.

practice: Walk back through the last day or two and notice, without scolding yourself, the tug of a first step: wanting a little more, wanting to be seen, needing to be right.
Then look for one moment that leaned the other way, like letting someone else take the credit. If you pray, ask, as the Exercises do, for the grace to be received under Christ's standard.

wordCard.voice: Two standards. Two banners on two fields, each with a plan in three small steps: riches, honor, pride; or poverty, insult, humility. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish, the language Ignatius wrote in: two banners, two flags.

carryVoice: Your line: under his standard. The first banner rarely looks evil; it can look like a nicer car. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: No man can serve two masters.
